newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy cannot afford to drop quest for EMU in 1999.
newsitem.headline: Italy cannot afford to drop quest for EMU in 1999.

text.p: Italy cannot afford to give up the fight to join a single European currency by its planned start date of 1999 but some economists believe it might be in its best interests to put off membership for a year or two.

The government has moved into high gear to whip the economy into shape for European economic and monetary union (EMU) but doubts are growing among Italy's partners, notably Germany, over its readiness to cope with the rigours of currency union.

Bankers meeting in Davos over the weekend said they were worried the debate over whether Italy and Spain should be among first participants in the Euro-currency would unsettle financial markets unless it was resolved soon.

Concerns are focusing on Italy's ability to the maintain the momentum for economic reform even if it succeeds in its goal of wrestling the ratio of public sector debt to three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) by the end of 1997.

That is one of the key criteria laid down in the 1991 Maastricht treaty, charting the road to monetary union, which Italy must meet if it is to have a chance of making the grade for the European currency club.

"This is a question of sustainability," said Ken Wattret, an economist with Paribas in London. "It is hard to believe Germany would accept Italy (in the first group of EMU members) given the potential instability for the euro," said Wattret.
Others believe Italy, which is still grappling with an inefficient state sector and a bloated pensions system, has much to gain from postponing its entry into EMU by one or two years.

"If Italy agreed to a delay of two years it would not be so bad," said Carmen Nuzzo, an economist with U.S. investment bank Salomon Brothers. "It would allow the authorities to correct the structural imbalances in the economy more gradually and more sustainably."

But few believe that the government can afford to throw in the towel now that it is asking Italians to accept major sacrifices -- higher taxes and low economic growth -- in the name of currency union.

"The government is in the hands of people who want to be in," said Sergio Romano, an ex-diplomat and newspaper pundit. "A delay is not as easy to arrange as people suggest. No one quite knows what will happen to those who stay out."

Abandonment of all effort to join EMU in 1999 could trigger a rout on the financial markets, where Italian bond prices are already under pressure because of the doubts over Italy's chances of climbing on board at the planned start date.

Italy has more to gain than any other country from EMU because the lower interest rates that it will bring would secure a lasting reduction in the cost of servicing a national debt of around 2,000 trillion lire ($1.25 trillion).

After rail-roading a 62.5 trillion lire budget through parliament at the end of last year the government is getting ready to slice a further 15 trillion lire from the deficit with a package of supplementary measures.
"Italy will continue to talk tough. They will try to resist and do their level best to create an economic situation that makes exclusion impossible," said Wattret.
"It is probably not feasible to keep taxes high and admit at the same time that there is going to be a delay. It is best for Italy to continue to push for 1999 entry," he added.
The most plausible scenario is for a delay of a year or two to be negotiated in 1998 when the European Commission pronounces on who has qualified among the EMU front-runners, economists said.
"If there is a delay it will be negotiated with strict guidelines. How it is presented to the financial markets will be very important," Nuzzo said.
